title: Why Have Indians Become a Regular Target of Hate in Singapore?
gist: Traces Singapore's anti-communal architecture — English as the language of state despite a 75 percent ethnic Chinese majority, four official languages, and the Ethnic Integration Policy imposed after the deadly 1964 race riots — as the baseline against which present-day hostility toward Indians must be judged.

insights.claim: When Singapore left the Malaysian Federation on August 9, 1965, Lee Kuan Yew made English rather than Chinese the primary language of government and education despite 75 percent of the population being ethnic Chinese.
insights.speaker: Asif Ullah Khan
insights.so_what: Singapore's social stability is a deliberate policy construct, not a natural equilibrium; erosion of that construct is a political risk factor for a major financial hub.
insights.locator: When Lee Kuan Yew took Singapore out of the Malaysian Federation

insights.claim: Singapore granted Malay, Mandarin and Tamil official status alongside English specifically so that ethnic minorities would not feel alienated by the majority-Chinese demographic reality.
insights.speaker: Asif Ullah Khan
insights.so_what: The multilingual settlement is the formal guarantee minorities point to; disputes over its erosion are the leading indicator of communal strain.
insights.locator: Ensuring that other ethnic minorities did not feel alienated

insights.claim: The 1964 race riots in Singapore left 36 people dead and directly prompted the dismantling of the colonial-era system in which different ethnic groups lived in isolated enclaves.
insights.speaker: Asif Ullah Khan
insights.so_what: Singapore's integration machinery was built in response to lethal violence, which explains the state's low tolerance for communal rhetoric today.
insights.locator: After the race riots in 1964 that left 36 people dead

insights.claim: Singapore's Ethnic Integration Policy requires every residential building to contain a mix of Chinese, Malay and Indian residents matching the country's actual population, making enforced residential mixing a structural rather than voluntary feature.
insights.speaker: Asif Ullah Khan
insights.so_what: A reusable model for states trying to engineer against segregation; also a reminder that hostility surfacing despite such tools signals pressures the policy cannot reach.
insights.quote: every building must have a mix of Chinese, Malay, and Indian residents that matches the country’s actual population

insights.claim: Because residential integration and multilingual official status are legally mandated in Singapore, any rise in anti-Indian hostility there has to originate outside the housing and language mechanisms the state controls.
insights.speaker: Asif Ullah Khan
insights.so_what: Points attention toward immigration flows, labor competition and online discourse rather than formal policy failure as the driver of communal friction.
insights.locator: This ensured that every building must have a mix
